title: MCP Discovery Feed
summary: Real-time dashboard that monitors GitHub for new MCP server releases, scores them by star velocity, and lets developers preview schemas and wishlist tools.
description: Developers tracking the fast-moving MCP ecosystem spend hours manually searching GitHub for new servers. MCP Discovery Feed aggregates new MCP server repositories in real time, ranks them by recent star velocity, and lets visitors browse a filterable card feed. Each card shows the tool's purpose, JSON schema preview, and a one-click install command copy. A localStorage wishlist lets developers bookmark tools to revisit.
keyFeatures: GitHub API polling for repos tagged 'mcp-server' with star-velocity ranking
JSON schema viewer showing available tool definitions inline
One-click install command generator (npx / pip / cargo)
localStorage wishlist with export to a plain text list
Category filters: AI, DevOps, Data, Productivity
whyInteresting: MCP adoption is accelerating in 2026 but discovery remains fragmented. This fills a real gap for AI agent developers without requiring any backend infrastructure, making it deployable as a pure static site.
inspiredBy: GitHub trending surge in AI agent tool registries and local-first developer tooling trends in 2026

title: Live Refactor Wall
summary: Classroom projection tool that connects to the teacher's VS Code, shows student code alongside an AI-generated refactor, and lets the class vote in real time whether to accept each suggestion.
description: Instructors teaching code quality often lack a participatory way to demonstrate refactoring decisions. Live Refactor Wall streams a selected code snippet from VS Code to a shared class display. Claude instantly proposes a refactored version with diff highlighting. Students join via a room code on their phones and vote Accept or Reject with an optional one-word reason. The aggregate vote and top reasons appear on the projection in real time, turning passive demos into classroom dialogue.
keyFeatures: VS Code extension that sends the active selection to the backend on demand
Claude API call for refactored version with structured diff output
WebSocket broadcast to all connected student browsers
Real-time Accept/Reject vote with reason tag cloud
Session replay log exportable as a Markdown discussion summary
whyInteresting: Refactoring judgment is hard to teach passively. Making it a live class vote surfaces diverse student intuitions and gives instructors immediate formative data on what reasoning students are applying.

title: Pair-to-Solo Bridge
summary: Analyzes pair programming session logs to identify which partner understood which concepts, then auto-generates personalized follow-up exercises for each student.
description: After pair programming sessions, instructors have no easy way to know which partner truly grasped each concept versus who was along for the ride. Pair-to-Solo Bridge takes session transcripts and git diffs, uses Claude to infer understanding signals per contributor, and generates a short personalized exercise set for each student targeting their specific gaps. Students receive a private link to their exercise set; instructors see an aggregate heatmap of which concepts the cohort still needs.
keyFeatures: Transcript upload (audio via Whisper or text paste) with speaker diarization
Git diff parsing to attribute lines and identify who drove each change
Claude API inference of per-student concept coverage from combined signals
Personalized exercise generation with difficulty calibrated to inferred level
Instructor dashboard with cohort concept-coverage heatmap
Supabase for student records, exercise history, and access-controlled links
whyInteresting: Pair programming's learning benefits depend on both students engaging, but that is hard to verify. This bridges the gap between the collaborative session and individual mastery, making pair programming pedagogically accountable.

title: CSTutorBench Personalization Gap: Submission-History-Grounded LLM Tutoring for CS1
summary: Extend the CSTutorBench evaluation framework by adding a submission-history adapter that grounds LLM tutoring responses in each student's prior attempt patterns, then measure whether this closes the personalization gap the benchmark identified.
description: CSTutorBench (SIGCSE TS 2026) benchmarks LLMs as CS tutors across accuracy, clarity, personalization, and interactive scaffolding. Its key finding is that LLMs approach human performance on accuracy and clarity but fall notably short on personalization. This project builds a lightweight personalization adapter on top of an existing LLM tutor: it retrieves the student's recent submission history from Jolly Feedback (Pisan's CSS 142/143 infrastructure), constructs a misconception profile, and injects it as structured context before each tutoring turn. The same CSTutorBench rubric is then re-applied to measure the delta, and the adapter design is reported as a reusable component.
keyFeatures: Jolly Feedback submission-log parser producing per-student misconception profiles
Context-injection layer wrapping any CSTutorBench-compatible LLM tutor
Automated re-evaluation on CSTutorBench's personalization and scaffolding dimensions
Ablation: profile depth (last 3 vs last 10 submissions) vs personalization score
Qualitative analysis of 20 student sessions comparing baseline and adapted tutor responses
whyInteresting: Personalization is the acknowledged weak spot of LLM tutors, and submission history is an underused signal that CS courses already collect. Closing this gap with existing infrastructure offers a publishable, replicable contribution grounded in real classroom data.
